title: Body Odor: You Stink
summary: Josh and Chuck explore body odor: why people have distinct odor types, how eccrine and apocrine sweat glands work, and how skin bacteria produce the smell. They cover sex and age differences in stinkiness, the controversial and shaky claims about racial body odor, and folk ideas such as the Elizabethan love apple. The hosts review remedies (trimming hair, baking soda, vinegar, boric acid), antiperspirant versus deodorant and aluminum concerns, the history of the term "B.O." and early deodorant ads, and medical odor conditions like maple syrup urine disease, trimethylaminuria, and bromhidrosis. The episode ends with listener mail about fencing in film and corrections to earlier episodes.
topics: stuff you should know body odor

segments.title: Opening banter and odor types
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the episode and introduce the idea that everyone has a unique odor type, which researchers can use to identify people, even with masking attempts. They mention mouse studies and the lab methods used to analyze scent.

segments.title: Eccrine and apocrine sweat glands
segments.summary: The hosts explain that eccrine sweat is mostly water and electrolytes for cooling and does not smell, while apocrine sweat carries cellular debris and milky secretions. Bacteria on the skin break down these compounds into smelly fatty acids. Apocrine glands develop at puberty, and babies do not produce them.

segments.title: Sex, age, and race differences in odor
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why men tend to smell more than women, linking testosterone and sweating efficiency, and cite a Japanese study on women training to sweat earlier. They then discuss claims about racial differences in body odor, noting that the supporting data is old and the claims are controversial.

segments.title: Japanese odor products and family scents
segments.summary: The hosts describe Japanese products, including a deodorant suit with silver ions and a fatty acid linked to old people's smell. Chuck reflects on how his mother's home smells like his grandparents' house, possibly due to inherited odor type.

segments.title: Scent in mate selection and folk odor customs
segments.summary: The hosts revisit claims that women can detect scent cues about reproductive partners and call the research overreaching. They then cover unverified customs, including a New Guinea armpit rubbing goodbye, an Austrian Tyrol handkerchief dance, and Elizabethan love apples soaked in armpit sweat.

segments.title: History of B.O. and early deodorant ads
segments.summary: The term B.O. is traced to a 1919 advertising campaign for Odorono deodorant, whose ads were openly sexist. The hosts mention early products like Mum and Tussy and the sprinkle-on Gold Bond.

segments.title: Hygiene tips and natural remedies
segments.summary: The hosts advise trimming underarm hair, keeping the body neat, and bathing within an hour before an interview since anxiety triggers apocrine sweating. Natural remedies include boric acid, vinegar, baking soda, rosemary oil, and tea tree oil, which work by changing skin pH or killing bacteria.

segments.title: Antiperspirants, deodorants, and aluminum concerns
segments.summary: The hosts explain that antiperspirants use aluminum compounds to plug sweat glands, while deodorants only mask odor. They discuss studies linking aluminum to breast cancer and Alzheimer's, which remain unproven, and mention deodorant formats such as sticks, gels, and crystal stones.

segments.title: Medical conditions that change body odor
segments.summary: The hosts cover conditions that change how a person smells: maple syrup urine disease, ketoacidosis breath, trimethylaminuria (fish odor), and phenylketonuria (musty barn smell). They also note asparagus urine odor, which they covered in a video podcast.

segments.title: Hyperhidrosis and bromhidrosis
segments.summary: The hosts describe hyperhidrosis, which causes excessive sweating treated by iontophoresis, Botox, and surgery. They define bromhidrosis as the fear of body odor, which can lead to excessive showering and has been linked to OCD, and Josh describes his own fear of poop smells.

segments.title: Listener mail: stage fencing in film
segments.summary: A listener who fenced in college explains show fencing, also called flynning after Errol Flynn, and recommends films with accurate swordplay: The Three Musketeers, Terms of Endearment-era rapier scenes (Riding in Cars with Boys is named by the hosts), and Ridley Scott's The Duellists. The hosts also mention a Count of Monte Cristo omission and corrections to earlier episodes on beer and cover band licensing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts share contact information and mention the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
